strengths: Novel problem formulation addressing genuine gap: prior-flexible amortised inference without retraining is an important practical problem with clear motivation and positioning relative to prior work.

Strong empirical results: dramatic speedups (orders of magnitude in sequential inference, milliseconds vs minutes), competitive or superior performance on static benchmarks, and demonstrable utility across diverse domains (GP hyperpriors, quantum systems, sensor fusion, stochastic volatility).

Original application to sequential inference: First amortised method to enable constant-time filtering while maintaining approximate conjugacy, showing ~50× speedup vs particle filters with comparable accuracy.

Technically sound methodology: Proposition 3.1 correctly links training loss to KL-divergence minimisation; change-of-measure framework is appropriate; Algorithm 1 is clear; comprehensive ablations (prior loss, error accumulation, meta-prior robustness) support design choices.

Honest limitations discussion and comprehensive appendix: Thoughtfully acknowledges scaling constraints, meta-prior requirements, and error accumulation; extensive experimental details aid reproducibility; ablations in Appendix C demonstrate rigor.

Elegant architecture design: Representing distributions as tokenised GMM sequences for transformer processing is creative; maintaining permutation invariance through removing positional encodings is principled.
weaknesses: Inadequate exploration of high-dimensional scaling limitations in main text: Figure 8 shows significant degradation with dimensionality (quadratic in components k, quadratic in dimension d), but this critical constraint is relegated to appendix. Insufficient evidence that real high-dimensional problems can be tackled effectively despite claims.

Meta-prior specification is a significant practical limitation with insufficient analysis: Requires well-specified meta-prior during training; only one misspecification scenario tested (Table 5); claims of 'robustness' lack supporting evidence; guidance on meta-prior construction is missing.

Theoretical justification for design choices is weak: Prior loss term ℓ_θ^prior introduced as necessary for 'latent space conjugacy' without explaining why this form is optimal; omission of positional encodings justified by permutation equivariance but not demonstrated as optimal; hyperparameter choices (6 layers, 64 latent dim) lack ablation.

'Approximate conjugacy' terminology is misleading: Not true Bayesian conjugacy; really just maintaining parametric family. Error accumulation analysis (C.5) shows degradation to ~95% information at depth 100, indicating conjugacy approximation breaks down at longer horizons. Practical implications inadequately discussed.

Baseline selection could be stronger: SVI from 2013 is dated; PFN-15 performs poorly, suggesting inadequate configuration; missing comparisons to recent diffusion-based and flow-based amortised inference methods mentioned in related work; no modern neural filtering methods for sequential experiments.

Limited guidance for practical deployment: No systematic method for choosing number of GMM components k; hyperparameter sensitivity claimed to be weak but not demonstrated; computational/memory requirements mentioned only in passing; sheer complexity (Table 8) creates high reimplementation barrier.

Insufficient failure case and robustness analysis: No systematic study of when method fails (multimodal posteriors, poor GMM approximation, observations far from meta-prior support); minimal analysis of sensitivity to observation noise; generalization to unseen GMM component counts (C.4) is limited.

Experimental design details raise concerns: Table 1 shows PFN-15 with extremely high variance (331.5±646.6), suggesting numerical instability rather than fair comparison; Experiment 4.1 kept ACE prior hyperparameters fixed while randomizing for others; quantum system uses simplified version.

Incremental novelty: Individual components (GMMs, transformers for inference, meta-learning) are not new; primary contribution is their combination and prior-flexibility aspect, which is valuable but somewhat incremental rather than introducing fundamentally new concepts.

strengths: Addresses important gap: Prior-flexible sequential inference with maintained conjugacy is underexplored and practically valuable
Well-designed permutation-equivariant architecture that respectfully combines transformers with GMM representations
Comprehensive experimental suite spanning analytical verification, intractable posteriors, and sequential inference across diverse domains
Substantial computational speedups (milliseconds vs. seconds/minutes compared to SVI)
Honest discussion of limitations including high-dimensional challenges, meta-prior sensitivity, and error accumulation
Extensive supplementary material with detailed ablations and reproducibility information
weaknesses: Core concept of 'approximate conjugacy' is never formally defined and remains empirically unvalidated; error accumulation (Figure 9) contradicts conjugacy claims
Meta-prior sensitivity is severe (Table 5: 40× degradation on out-of-sample meta-prior), undermining the central 'prior-flexibility' claim
Baseline comparisons are unfair: PFNs handicapped by marginalization over meta-prior; TabPFNv2 much larger and pretrained; no comparison with amortised SBI methods
Sequential inference claims overstate capabilities: only two experiments, no comparison with amortised alternatives, DTs underperform PF on accuracy, error accumulation non-negligible

Fundamental scalability limitation: memory O(d²) in latent dimension; most experiments ≤24D; Figure 8 shows polynomial degradation; applicability severely limited for realistic high-dimensional problems
Limited novelty: straightforward combination of established techniques (transformers, GMMs, meta-learning); Proposition 3.1 is trivial

Practical usability concerns: requires well-specified meta-prior p(φ) without guidance; hyperparameter tuning superficial ('limited manual tuning'); reproducibility limited (code unavailable, preliminary analyses)
Table 7 contradicts claimed component invariance: noticeable degradation (0.0873→0.0946) when doubling components despite architectural invariance claims

strengths: Novel architecture combining GMMs and transformers for prior-flexible amortised Bayesian inference with approximate conjugacy—uniquely enabling sequential inference without retraining, a capability no existing amortised method provides

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental validation across diverse problem types (analytical verification, non-conjugate posteriors, quantum systems, sequential inference) with strong baselines and careful metrics
Significant practical impact with massive speedups (minutes to milliseconds) while matching or exceeding baseline performance, demonstrated across multiple applications
Solid theoretical foundation with Proposition 3.1 rigorously connecting the training objective to KL divergence minimization and clear justification of the permutation-invariant architecture design

Excellent reproducibility: code on GitHub, extensive appendices with all experimental details, comprehensive ablation studies, and honest discussion of limitations including meta-prior specification issues and error accumulation
The permutation-invariant use of GMMs as unordered token sequences is elegant and natural, providing both expressive power and structural constraints beneficial for sequential composition
weaknesses: Scalability limitations insufficiently addressed: GMMs struggle in high dimensions (O(d²) memory complexity for full covariance), most experiments ≤10D latent variables, and only comparison on high-dimensional problems is against SVI which also degrades

Meta-prior specification adds practical complexity; Table 5 shows notable degradation on out-of-distribution meta-priors (0.0003→0.0054), but only one misspecification experiment provided and robustness poorly characterized

Sequential inference error accumulation inadequately characterized: Figure 9 suggests degradation begins around depth 30-40, not just at depth 70, with limited guidance on practical sequence length limits; experiments only at moderate depths

Design choice justifications lacking: limited ablation on architectural hyperparameters (6 layers, 64 dimension, 8 heads), why cross-entropy softmax for weights, and Table 7 (GMM component generalization) only provides preliminary evidence on linear Gaussian setting

Approximate conjugacy claim needs clarification: 'approximate conjugacy' is not formally defined, and Table 6 shows modest posterior KL improvement (0.0004→0.0004) from prior loss despite claims of criticality for sequential inference

Limited exploration of failure modes: no analysis of performance on highly multimodal posteriors with disparate component scales, unclear how GMM approximation degrades in adversarial settings, sample-space transformation f(·) mentioned but not thoroughly analyzed

Incomplete comparison with recent prior-flexible methods: ACE only marginally outperformed in some cases (Table 1: 0.0094 vs 0.0003), some baseline comparisons potentially unfair (PFNs marginalizing meta-prior), sensitivity-aware amortised inference mentioned but not quantitatively compared

Limited high-dimensional evaluation: C.1 shows degradation on conjugate problems up to 24D, quantum/stochastic volatility experiments (10D) are most challenging but modest by modern standards; unclear scaling to 50+ dimensional latents
